segments.text: Questions from members, and we have read your submission. But over to you.
Thank you. Kia ora koutou.
I'm a lawyer based in Nelson.
And so I want to make a couple of points in my oral
submission. The first is that, contrary to
suggestions I've seen in some quarters,
the Supreme Court's decision here is not a novel
one. The tort of public nuisance is an old
area of law.
It's been applied to
environmental issues in the past.
There are a bunch of cases in Victorian
times on water pollution
arising from industrialization.
And the cases were quite clear that the fact that you're only
contributing maybe a limited amount to the pollution, and there'd still be
pollution if you just took away your individual contributions, that
isn't a barrier to being found liable for public
nuisance. So actually, in my view, the court's decision was quite orthodox in just
applying old principles of law to a new
context.
So I think that that's something to bear in mind when it comes to whether
it's justifiable to
legislate to override this court
decision on this old area of law,
when we're talking about one of the greatest challenges we
face as a planet and as
humanity.
The other thing I'd like to say is around the retrospective nature of the
legislation. And in this case, it's not just
retrospectively taking away people's
right to sue and to get a remedy for public nuisance.
It's also interfering with
existing court proceedings, court proceedings
that are currently in existence
and before the courts. Even when Parliament
legislates retrospectively,
it normally excludes proceedings
that are already before the courts.
That's because
while retrospective legislation, of course, always raises issues in
terms of the rule of law, but there are particularly grave issues in terms of the
rule of law and separation of powers when you're interfering with
court cases that are in existence before the courts.
And so that's the points that I want to make.
Thank you very much. We've got a question from Dr. Deborah Russell.
Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Daniel.
Would you see a problem with Parliament legislating after the
completion of Mike Smith's case?
Well, I think that would be
a better way to do it. If you
felt, after the outcome of that case, that
legislation was necessary, of course, Parliament could legislate.
But then it would know what it's actually legislating to,
what the actual issue is with the law.
Because at the moment, all the Supreme Court said is, "Well, this case can
go forward to trial, and we can have a full judgment.
It's not untenable."
But we don't know whether it will succeed or not.
We don't know what the law will look like at the end of that.
And actually, interfering with pending
cases before the courts is a pretty extraordinary step for
Parliament to take.
Thank you.
Fantastic. Well, thank you, Daniel. Nice to see you again.
And thank you both for your written and your oral submission. We appreciate it.
Thanks.
Okay, members, we now come to Lawyers for Climate
Action. And
let's just see who we have got here. We've got Jennie.
And who else is going to be with you, Jennie, or is it just yourself?
Laura McKay. So I don't know whether she's able to be on screen at
the same time, but I can hand over to her when I'm finished.
That might be-
Okay. We do have Laura on here, so
up to you.
Jennie, you've got 10 minutes. We have read your written submission.
But please do leave some time at the end for questions. Over to you.
Thank you. We'll try to do that. Well, kia ora koutou.
My name is Jennie Cooper. I'm here in my capacity as president of Lawyers for
Climate Action. And as we were just mentioning, I'm here together with
our acting executive director, Laura McKay.
So Lawyers for Climate Action NZ is opposed to the bill.
We say it's a disproportionate knee-jerk reaction to one
case which has yet to be decided.
It goes against the interests of every single person in New Zealand except
the major emitters who lobbied for it.
The reason we say that is because everyone suffers the consequences of
climate change,
such as the damage caused by extreme weather events and sea level rise.
But based on this bill, everyone will be left paying for those
consequences without any opportunity to seek redress from those
most responsible.
It is bad law based on bad policy, and it's the result
of a deeply flawed decision-making process.
I'd like to start with a few comments on the process.
First of all, the bill does appear to be a direct response to secret
lobbying by Z Energy and Fonterra.
It would appear that at their request, the government is seeking to step in to
decide private litigation in favor of powerful corporate
interests.
Now, whatever you think about Mr. Smith's claim, whatever you think about the role
of tort law should be in relation to climate change, that sets a
dangerous precedent. This bill is an infringement of the rights of Mr.
Smith, and it is also directly contrary to the rule of law.
Secondly, the process for the introduction of this bill has been
unacceptably rushed. There's been no proper consultation, including no
consultation with Maori, and the opportunity for public debate has been
seriously curtailed. Setting a 10-day submission period
closing at 9:00 a.m. after a long weekend sends a clear message that
the proponents of this bill have no real interest in public feedback,
despite this being a vitally important issue of public interest.
So we say that's a serious concern, because this bill not only takes away Mr.
Smith's claim, but it would effectively impose a total restriction on
anyone's ability to bring a claim for damages caused by any event where
climate change is a contributing factor, and I'll come back to that, but it does
appear that the implications of this don't appear to have been recognized or
thought through. And we say that this rushed process is
completely unnecessary. Mr. Smith's claim has been on foot since
2000. There has been adequate time to consider its
implications. The Supreme Court decision saying it should go to trial was issued
two years ago. There's no good reason why this issue is now being
addressed with urgency.
Should I pause for questions? I do have more points to make.
What is the procedure?
Make all the points and then we'll have the questions at the end.
Great. Thank you.
Turning to why it's bad policy. Well, first of all, the stated
reason for the bill is to avoid the risk of a parallel regime to the Climate Change
Response Act. There is no such risk for the reasons that the Supreme
Court held, which is that the Climate Change Response Act does not address
issues of compensation, liability for harm,
and redress the issues that Mr. Smith's claim raises and the
issues which tort law addresses. So there's nothing in
the act that addresses those issues or that will be contradicted by that.
There is nothing in legislation that deals with the question of who is
able to claim for compensation and who is liable to pay for compensation
for the harm caused by climate change, which includes harm from
weather-related events such as floods,
droughts, slips, storms, and fires, which we are seeing with increasing
regularity.
Now, who can claim and who should pay for these losses are difficult and
complex questions.
It's very arguable that they should be addressed by legislation, but
we do not have any legislation that addresses that.
Rather than developing suitable legislation to fill this gap, this
bill simply says that there is no accountability for major emitters
and no way for those suffering from climate harm to seek
redress. Secondly, the bill is said to be
aimed at ensuring certainty for business.
We say it will have the opposite effect, and Laura will touch on that
briefly as well.
Finally, from me, why the bill is bad law.
It's clear the drafting process has been rushed.
The scope of the bill is extraordinarily wide and likely to have unintended
consequences. For example, it protects emitters from
liability for any damage to the extent that it was or may
have been, in whole or in part, directly or indirectly
caused or contributed to by climate change.
In effect, that means that anyone who contributes to climate change
cannot be sued for any damage caused in New Zealand by
any extreme weather-related event, such as a storm, a
flood, et cetera, because all of those events will have
been at least partly contributed to by climate change.
Now, this bar appears to apply
regardless of whether the person to be sued's emissions
are the reason they are being sued or some other reason.
So for example, if an emitter of greenhouse gases
also negligently fails to maintain a stop bank or fails to
remove forestry slash and thereby causes a risk of damage to the
neighbor's property, based on the wording of this bill, they won't be able
to be sued for the damage that may cause if a severe weather event
is also a contributing factor to the damage.
And I don't believe any consideration has been given to the consequences of that.
Finally from me, before I hand over to Laura,
I would ask the members of this committee to step back
and reflect on the fact that the bill before them would
explicitly protect emitters everywhere in the world from
any form of liability to anyone in New Zealand
for, quote, "Threats to the continuation of a safe
and habitable climate system."
Ask yourselves whose interests such a law would serve and how it
could possibly be justified in the public interest.
Thank you, and I'll hand over to Laura.
Thanks, Jenny.
Kia ora, Jenny.
So there's three more key impacts of the bill I'd like to note.
Those relate to the inconsistency of the bill with the Treaty of Waitangi, also
with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and also with New Zealand's international
obligations. Not going to go through our submission, but I do want to highlight a
few key points. So first relating to the Treaty of Waitangi.
In addition to the point that Jenny's already made about the rushed and inadequate
process, it's important to note that at least according to the regulatory impact
statement, there's been no consultation with Maori.
That regulatory impact statement itself acknowledges that this is likely
inconsistent with the Crown's Treaty of Waitangi obligations.
The Crown's provided no good reason for rushing through this bill and no good
reason why it's failed to engage with Maori on a bill with such significant impact.
I think that's particularly important to note in light of the lobbying for this
bill from some of the defendants in the Smith and Ponteria case.
As noted in our submissions, if this bill is to proceed, then at a very minimum,
a full consultation process should be undertaken, and particularly with Maori.
Secondly, in relation to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, we've set out in our
submission some of the minimum rights that the bill undermines, but one in
particular I want to highlight.
Under Section 8 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, no one shall be deprived of
life except on such grounds as are established by law and are consistent with the
principles of fundamental justice.
So as noted in our submission, the courts have been steadily developing an
understanding of climate change as a threat to the right of life But in
this case, the right to life is actually explicitly recognized in the bill
because it bars a range of emissions related climate change effects,
including endangering or impairing the life, safety,
health, property, or comfort of the public.
It's really difficult to understand why unproven concerns about certainty
for business would be prioritized over the right to life for New Zealand citizens.
Given that the justifications for this bill have no basis, and also given the
significant constitutional risks, the grounds for this bill are clearly not
consistent with the principles of fundamental justice that's required by Section 8
of NZ BORA.
Thirdly, I just want to highlight specifically the bill's inconsistency with New
Zealand's free trade agreements.
That's particularly so the EU-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement and the
UK-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement.
Both of those free trade agreements contain non-regression clauses.
So, for example, under Article 19.24 of the New
Zealand-EU Free Trade Agreement, a party shall not weaken or
reduce the levels of protection afforded in its environmental or labor law in
order to encourage trade or investment.
So what's extraordinary then is that the government's been quite clear that the
purpose of the bill is to encourage investment, and that clearly engages this
article.
It's important to note that this bill is not an abstract risk to this free trade
agreement. There's mechanisms within the EU through which EU civil
society can and already does raise breaches, and New Zealand's
backtracking has already been raised within the EU domestic advisory group and
within the UK.
This creates significant risk for New Zealand exporters.
So finally, I just want to emphasize that point that this cumulative
inconsistency with so many key international obligations, particularly our free
trade agreements, seriously threatens not only New Zealand's clean, green
reputation, but also our reputation as a stable democracy with a
strong rule of law and access to justice.
That has the potential to create more uncertainty for businesses and international
investors than a court ruling that would've gone through a long, independent,
considered, and evidence-based process.
Thank you.
Thank you, Laura, and thank you, Jennie.
We do have a couple of people with questions, but unfortunately, we have met our
full 10-minute allocation for you, so I'm sorry we won't be able to have them.
But we do appreciate you both submitting to us today and also for your written
submission on the bill as well. So thank you.
Jennie, I'll drop you a note.
Thank you very much. Now, Ms-
Mr. Chair, I wonder if they're still there, this is one of the

I'd seek leave for just a couple of minutes of questions.

five or 10 minutes depending on it, and please do allow time for questions.

Your submission's excellent. You acknowledge there's no regime for compensation or
liability currently, and also that there are real
complexities. In extinguishing
this right of people to take tort claims,
is this a big missed opportunity to use the knowledge and the
expertise and the intelligence of the courts to find a way
through
using the development of common law?

for, us to actually use the courts to find
us the way through?
Yes, absolutely, and the point I'd just like to make is that the courts are well
experienced in doing that, so that is the whole purpose of the tort law and the
common law is to find remedies to these types of problems.
Another really important point is that the Supreme Court expressly recognized the
importance of tikanga in the development of this, and this statutory
bar expressly,
forbids that from proceeding. So it halts the court's ability to develop
the common law as it relates to tikanga Maori as well.
So I would agree with you, Steve.
Thank you.
Thanks, Steve. Thank you, Laura and Jennie. Really appreciate your time today.

I'm Simon Tucker, Fonterra's group director of Global
External Affairs. And joining me is our director of sustainability,
Charlotte Rutherford.
And thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
To be clear at the outset, Fonterra supports this legislation.
This is an important issue for our business, for our farmer owners, and we
believe for New Zealand as a whole.
Fonterra and five other companies are facing a lawsuit where the High
Court is being asked to override Parliament's legislative
framework for managing greenhouse gas emissions.
The lawsuit seeks to order us to immediately cut greenhouse
gas emissions to net zero.
In practice, if this were to happen, we would need to
immediately cease operations. This would have
devastating economic, environmental, and social impacts,
as explained in our written comments.
Analysis commissioned by several of the businesses involved, including
Fonterra, found that the impact on New Zealand's GDP from this
lawsuit in the first year could be more than twice the GDP
decline New Zealand experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic in
Fonterra believes strongly that Parliament should set the framework for how
New Zealand achieves its emissions reduction goals, not the courts.
We do not believe a court case brought by a private individual
which attempts to create a parallel judicial emissions regime
is the right way to address such a fundamental public policy matter.
Our view about the severity of this issue is longstanding, as is
our view that this is an issue for Parliament to resolve.
As you would expect, given the seriousness of this for Fonterra,
for our farmer owners, and for New Zealand,
we have shared these views publicly and with stakeholders from across the
political spectrum over several years.
We do acknowledge that in one case, while working on this issue, a
Fonterra staff member sent a document to a Beehive staff member's personal
email address.
This was inappropriate and contrary to our internal
policies.
This should not distract us from the key issue.
It is Parliament, not the courts, that should set emissions reduction
targets for New Zealand.
Before I close my comments, let me just emphasize that Fonterra's
support for this bill should not be mistaken for a lack of
commitment to climate action.
Fonterra has credible emission reduction targets in place that have
been internationally assessed as being aligned to limiting global
warming to 1.5 degrees.
We are investing hundreds of millions of dollars to continue our significant
decarbonization program.
For example, we are now coal-free in the North Island.
In fact, since 2018, shifting our manufacturing assets off
fossil fuels alone has had the same emission reduction impact
as taking almost 200,000 cars off New Zealand
roads.
We are also working closely with farmer shareholders and other partners
to address on-farm emissions and hit our Scope 3 targets.
This includes Fonterra being the largest private sector investor in AgriZero
NZ, with over $50 million committed.
Fonterra is proud of its world-class approach to emissions reduction
and remains committed to reducing our impact on the environment.
In closing, we would urge the committee to support this legislation
to ensure a nationally coordinated framework for New Zealand's
response to climate change.
Thank you, and happy to answer any questions.
Thanks, Simon. And just before I go to questions, just wanted to see.
Charlotte, do you have any comments you would like to make?
Nothing additional. Happy to move straight to comments. Thank you.
Thank you. We'll start with Dr. Deborah Russell.
Thank you, Chair. Hi, Simon and Charlotte. Nice to see you again.
A couple of things I want to talk about.
One is, Simon, you said in one scenario,
if the court case was upheld, eventually we would have to immediately
stop operations. It's a bit hyperbolistic, isn't it?
Well, that is what is the main central plank of the
plaintiff's case. If he didn't want to stop our operations,
he shouldn't have made that the central plank of his legal case.
Okay. I just feel as though that's, anyway, that's by the by.
Look, the other thing I really wanted to talk about was
our trade agreements and the extent to which
our
actions like this might further create concern around
whether or not we are meeting some of the obligations in our
free trade agreements, particularly with the UK and the EU.
Have you done any analysis of that?
We have done some looking at that, and I understand the government has as well.
To be honest, we're not particularly concerned about that in this situation,
Deborah, because, as I understand, as we understand those
trade agreements, it's about New Zealand fulfilling its obligations,
for example, to the Paris Accord.
And
I think it's pretty clear that Parliament has
passed the Climate Change Reduction Act, which will
seek to achieve that.
I would also note, as I did in my comments, that
we have set emissions reduction targets as a business, which
are also consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5
degrees. So, it's not an issue that we
are concerned about in this instance.
Okay. Thank you.
Thanks, Deborah. We've got a number of people with questions.
We'll go to Steve Abel.
Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Let me know if I'm cutting out at all.
When did you first lobby the government to
extinguish the right of not only Mike Smith,
but all New Zealanders to take Fonterra to
court for the harms caused by your climate pollution?
I think going back to the initiation of this case, we
were pretty public, Steve, in our comments to
the media, certainly to any politician who would listen
to us, that we thought that this case
was trying to do business that very properly believed
should be under the jurisdiction of Parliament.
We've made no secret of that position, and we've talked to political
stakeholders across
the spectrum over several years on that basis.
I wonder, how do you address
the articulations of deep concern
that that level of direct lobbying to the
Prime Minister's office
expresses an obedience to vested interests
of this government that
raises the accusation of corruption?
And how does that reflect on Fonterra as such
a major company in New Zealand, directly lobbying the Prime Minister's
office with private emails?
I mean, to be honest, we speak to the government, any government,
elected government in New Zealand literally hundreds of times a
year on issues. We are a big business, vertically
integrated across the New Zealand economy.
You want to talk about education and training, you want to talk about trade and
geopolitical risk, you want to talk about energy, transportation,
railways, ports, infrastructure, education.
We have interests in all of those issues, and we firmly believe that
government decision-making is best enabled by having good
position of the facts of both to help them
make good decisions and to understand the impacts of them.
So, this case was seeking to essentially
force New Zealand to stop Fonterra,
to cause us to cease operations. And we thought it was
important that the government understood how seriously that would
impact our farmers, farmers across New Zealand, our regional
communities, and the New Zealand economy.
So we were pretty clear about why we thought it was an important issue.
Thank you so much-
My final one, Mr. Chair, if that's all right, is that-
Sorry, Steve.
Is there currently-- I-
Sorry, Steve, there are a number of other people with questions, so I will need to
go to them in fairness.
Thank you.
We'll go to Carl Bate.
Thanks very much, Chair. Just in terms of the importance of Fonterra to New
Zealand, what amount of
taxation does Fonterra pay? And do you have any
estimate of what your wider dairy or
farmer providers pay into the system?
It's a fair question, Carl. I have to say, I don't know off the top of my head how
much tax is paid. I mean, I would just
observe, among other things, Fonterra is
responsible for very nearly a quarter of New Zealand's total exports,
that foreign exchange coming in. We know, for example, I think it was last year,
we paid out $16 billion to our farmer
owners. We know that they spend much of that into
regional New Zealand, so it does have a very positive impact on the New Zealand
economy.
So if Fonterra was to cease, all of the government's activity
and work across its environmental activity would be put at risk by
that
export earnings not happening and that contribution into the New Zealand taxpayer
also not earning, I would imagine?
Yeah, I think certainly if we were had to cease operations, there'd be
a lot of money, a lot of jobs. I mean, I think the other thing that we would
highlight is if New Zealand stopped producing dairy,
that dairy would be produced in some other part of the world.
So somewhat ironically, that would almost certainly happen with a higher carbon
footprint.
So what's the importance of having a clear pathway and
confidence that that's not a risk Fonterra or its
farmer producer base would face or could face?
Well, I think it comes back to the fact that it's Parliament that really
is the appropriate forum for these massively complicated
national questions to be resolved.
Okay. Well, thank you, Simon, and thank you, Charlotte, for joining us this
afternoon and for your written submission.
Mr. Chair. Mr. Chair, I wonder if we could allow a little leeway
on Fonterra, given they're the main player in this piece of
legislation, to ask a couple more questions.
We have already given them 13, 14 odd minutes, which is over their
10-minute allocation. Unfortunately, we'd be here for the rest of the day,
unfortunately, Steve. I am trying to be as fair as I reasonably can, and hence why
I gave questions to both you and Deborah to begin with.
But I'm doing my best. Doing my best.
But thank you, Simon and Charlotte.
Appreciate your time this afternoon.
We're now going to move to David.
David, great to see you. You're with us. David, we've read your submission.
You have five minutes. Please do leave some time for questions from members.
Tena koutou katoa. Thank you for the opportunity to speak
today. My name is David Laughlin. I'm a registered
architect based in Whangarei, Raglan, and I
appreciate the opportunity to briefly expand on my written submission.
When I first read this bill, I found myself asking a very simple
question: what problem is the bill trying to solve?
The answer I came to was that it seeks to prevent or significantly
reduce climate related tort claims.
That concerns me,
not because I expect a wave of litigation, but because
accountability is one of the foundations of a fair
society.
For a long time, our legal system has recognized a simple principle.
If someone's actions may have caused foreseeable harm,
those affected should have the opportunity to ask a court to
examine the evidence and decide the case on its merits.
This bill would remove that opportunity for an entire category of
claims before the facts can even be considered.
As an architect, I'm required to think well beyond the
present.
The buildings I design may still be standing in 50 or 100 years'
time.
Every decision carries consequences, and accepting
responsibility for those consequences is part of my
profession.
Climate change asks us to think in exactly the same way.
It asks us to consider not only what is convenient today, but
what we leave to those who come after us.
Much of my life has been spent being in or on coastlines,
forests, and rural landscapes across Aotearoa.
Those experiences have reinforced something I believe deeply.
Land and water are never simply economic assets.
They hold ecological relationships, cultural histories, and
communities that have developed over generations
When those relationships are damaged, the effects are rarely confined to
one place or one generation.
For that reason, I don't believe this bill will encourage better environmental
decision-making.
Instead, I'm concerned it sends the message that
reducing legal accountability
is an appropriate response to increasingly complex
environmental challenges.
New Zealand has generally sought to strengthen responsibility where
significant harm may occur.
In my view, this bill moves in the opposite direction.
For those reasons, I respectfully ask the committee to recommend the
bill not proceed.

up online.

but please do allow some time for members to ask questions.

Tēnā koe koutou.
Thank you for the opportunity to submit. My name is Lindis Jones.
I'm the Chief Executive of Z Energy.
With me is Patricia Green, Z's General Counsel, who will
take the committee through our submission in more detail.
We support this bill for three reasons.
First, climate policy should be set by Parliament, not the courts.
Climate change presents some of the most difficult choices our country faces.
How we reduce emissions affects jobs, household costs,
energy security, investment, and economic
resilience. Those are questions of public
policy that should be balanced by elected representatives on behalf of all
New Zealanders.
Second reason is that while climate litigation can have a certain appeal,
it is ultimately a poor substitute for climate policy.
Faced with a challenge as significant as climate change, it's understandable to
want a simple answer or a single party to hold accountable.
But New Zealand's energy transition will not be delivered company by company
or court case by court case.
It requires a coherent framework that balances competing interests,
weighs difficult trade-offs, and applies consistently across the economy.
We already have that framework in the hard-fought-for Climate Change Response Act
and the Emissions Trading Scheme.
Third,
certainty matters. New Zealand needs significant long-term investment to
support both energy security and the transition to lower
emissions forms of energy.
Clear, stable, and durable policy settings give
businesses the confidence to make these investments over very long
time horizons.
The reason we support this bill is not simply because Z is a defendant in the Smith
versus Fonterra litigation.
The issue at stake is much larger than that.
Clear, stable, and durable-- oh, sorry.
It's--
no? Just...
Cool.
I'll start again. The reason we support this bill is not simply because Z is a
defendant in the Smith v. Fonterra litigation.
The issue at stake is much larger than that.
Also, we're not here to comment on any individual or details of that specific
litigation.
Even if we weren't involved in those proceedings, we would still support the bill
because we believe climate policy works best when it is applied
consistently across the economy
rather than individually through court cases focused on a small number
of individual companies.
But also, let me be clear, our support for this bill should not be mistaken for a
lack of commitment to climate action.
We support New Zealand's transition to a lower emissions future and are investing
in that transition today.
Supporting this bill is about how climate policy is made,
not whether emissions should be reduced.
The fundamental question before the committee is not whether climate change
requires action.
It does. The question is, who should determine New Zealand's pathway forward?
And we fundamentally believe that responsibility sits properly
with a democratically elected parliament. Thank you for your time.
I'll hand to Patricia.
Thank you.
From a legal perspective, the claims before the courts remain novel and
unresolved.
The litigation seeks to establish forms of climate-related liability that have
not previously been recognized by New Zealand courts.
More recently, the remedies sought have expanded to include immediate
net zero obligations for the defendants.
We have presented the committee with evidence about the potential consequences of
those remedies. Independent modeling indicates that the
remedies sought against the defendants could reduce New Zealand's
GDP by at least $21.9 billion
over five years.
If similar obligations were extended across other businesses and
sectors, the impact could be substantially larger again.
This highlights the nature of the claims before the court.
